review.title: Exam 1 review guide
review.lead: The 20 questions from the Exam 1 review sheet and the 25 questions from Exam 1 itself, each with its answer written in plain steps, the answer first and then the reason.
review.note: The review sheet and the Exam 1 key are the professor's. The answers here say what the key says, in full sentences, with the middle steps filled in from the slides.

sets.title: Exam 1 review sheet · 20 questions
sets.about: Handed out before Exam 1 and answered in class on September 29. About 15 of the 25 exam questions came from this sheet with one thing changed.

items.question: What is the similarity between m in mad and b in bad, and what is the difference between those sounds?
items.answer: Both m and b are voiced, and both are made at the lips, so they share voicing and place of articulation. The difference is manner (how the air is let out). For m the velum (the soft back part of the roof of the mouth) is lowered, so the air comes out through the nose, and m is a nasal stop. For b the velum is raised, so the air is blocked completely at the lips and then released through the mouth, and b is an oral stop (a plosive).

items.question: What is the role of the learning rate in stochastic gradient descent and the role of stiffness in a viscous springy system? What happens when the learning rate is high versus low, and when stiffness is high versus low?
items.answer: The learning rate determines how big a fraction of each mistake gets corrected, and stiffness determines how strongly the spring pulls back toward equilibrium (its resting position). With a high learning rate, each correction is large, so the estimate reaches the right region fast but keeps jumping around it, so it is less accurate. With a low learning rate, each correction is small, so the estimate moves slowly but settles steadily, so it is more accurate but slow. With high stiffness, the spring pulls back hard, so it returns to equilibrium fast. With low stiffness, it pulls back weakly, so it returns slowly. In both systems a bigger setting means a faster response.

items.question: What is the physical principle behind how your auditory system hears different frequencies? Describe the basic physics of the basilar membrane to show how the system works.
items.answer: The principle is that frequency goes up with stiffness and down with mass. The basilar membrane (the long strip inside the cochlea) is heavy and loose at one end and light and stiff at the other end. The heavy, loose end vibrates most for low frequencies, because extra mass makes a part harder to move, so it vibrates more slowly. The light, stiff end vibrates most for high frequencies, because stiffness makes a part spring back faster, so it vibrates more quickly. Each place along the membrane is connected to its own neurons. So which neurons fire tells the brain which places are vibrating, and that tells the brain which frequencies are in the sound.

items.question: Two temperature control systems are set to 70. In the first, the thermostat is right next to the heating and cooling unit. When the temperature is above 70, the air conditioning turns on, the temperature drops to 70, and the thermostat detects that and turns the unit off. Below 70, the heat turns on until 70 and then stops. In the second, the thermostat is far from the unit. When the temperature is above 70, the air conditioning turns on, but the thermostat does not detect 70, so the temperature keeps dropping to 60. Then the heat turns on, the temperature rises past 70 to 80 before the thermostat notices, and so on. Which system is like a spring by itself, and which is like a mass-spring system?
items.answer: The first system, with the thermostat next to the unit, is like a spring by itself. This is because it moves toward its goal of 70 and stops there, the way a spring alone returns to equilibrium and stays. The second system, with the far thermostat, is like a mass-spring system. This is because it keeps going past 70, to 60 and then to 80, and swings back and forth around the goal. A moving mass keeps moving past equilibrium, so a mass-spring system overshoots and oscillates in the same way. The delay in detecting the temperature plays the part of the mass.

items.question: Why is the exhaustive algorithm so inefficient for solving the shortest path problem?
items.answer: The exhaustive algorithm is inefficient because it works out the total cost of every complete path separately. The paths overlap, so the same additions get done over and over. Every time a stage is added, the number of complete paths multiplies, so the work grows very fast. It does find the true shortest path, but for a big problem it takes far too long.

items.question: What are the different ways we distinguish between the consonants at the beginning of the words Pam, Bam, Dam, Tam, Kam and Gam?
items.answer: All six are oral stops, so they are distinguished by place of articulation and by voicing. Place is where the air is blocked. The p and b are made at the lips (labial), the t and d at the alveolar ridge behind the upper teeth (alveolar), and the k and g with the back of the tongue at the velum (velar). Voicing is whether the vocal folds vibrate. The p, t and k are voiceless, and the b, d and g are voiced. So each sound is one place combined with one voicing.

items.question: Describe the psychological principle of closure, and how it is used in the GPT system.
items.answer: Closure is the tendency to complete a familiar but unfinished pattern. A broken circle is still seen as a circle, and three black circles with wedges cut out are seen as a triangle, because the mind fills in what is missing. GPT uses the same idea as its way of learning, which is called the cloze task. A sentence is taken, part of it is hidden, and the network has to guess the missing word. If the guess is wrong, the weights are changed a little. After billions of these completions the network ends up knowing the language.

items.question: How is knowledge represented in neural networks?
items.answer: Knowledge is represented in the weights, which are the numbers on the connections between neurons. The weights determine how the input numbers get turned into the output probabilities. Changing the weights changes what the network knows, so learning means changing the weights. In the brain the same kind of knowledge sits in the synapses (the connections between neurons), and a large AI system can have trillions of weights.

items.question: What is the basic tradeoff that we see in both the shortest path problem and the stochastic gradient descent algorithm?
items.answer: The tradeoff is speed against accuracy. In the shortest path problem, the greedy algorithm is fast but can pick the wrong path, and the exhaustive algorithm always finds the right path but is slow. Dynamic programming balances the two. In stochastic gradient descent, a high learning rate reaches the right region fast but keeps jumping around it, and a low learning rate settles accurately but slowly.

items.question: What is my favorite popular way of describing how learning in AI works? Fake it till you make it. Describe why I describe it this way.
items.answer: The system starts with completely random weights, so at first it does not know anything. It is just faking it. It makes a guess, gets feedback on how wrong the guess was, and changes its weights a little so that it does better next time. After repeating this many times it makes it, which means it ends up with the right knowledge.

items.question: What is the output of an LLM or a neural network in general, and how does it express a decision?
items.answer: The output is a probability distribution over the possible categories. That is a list with one number per category, where each number is between 0 and 1 and all the numbers add up to 1. The decision is the category with the highest probability. For an LLM the categories are the possible next words, so the output says how likely each word is to come next.

items.question: Is this a good output of a neural network, if there are 4 categories, [.4, 0, .5, .2]? Why or why not?
items.answer: No, it is not a good output. This is because the output has to be a probability distribution, so the numbers have to add up to 1. These numbers add up to 1.1. Each number is between 0 and 1, so that part is fine, but the total is wrong.

items.question: In each vowel, does the air vibrate at a single frequency? Yes or no?
items.answer: No. The air in a vowel vibrates at a combination of frequencies at the same time. This is because the tongue shape changes where the air in the vocal tract is constricted (narrowed), so different parts of the air have different mass and stiffness. Different mass and stiffness means different frequencies, and they all sound together. The combination is what makes one vowel sound different from another.

items.question: What are the 2 basic ways we distinguish vowels?
items.answer: Vowels are distinguished by tongue height and by tongue frontness. Height is whether the tongue is high or low in the mouth. Frontness is whether the raised part of the tongue is toward the front or the back of the mouth. For example, the vowel in dean is high and front, the vowel in dune is high and back, the vowel in Dan is low and front, and the vowel in Don is low and back.

items.question: Some people say that everything is a harmonic oscillator. Give 5 examples of oscillatory systems we discussed in class or in the Meadows book.
items.answer: A mass on a spring swinging back and forth. The air in the vocal tract vibrating during speech, with its particles moving closer together and farther apart. The vocal folds opening and closing hundreds of times a second. The estimate in stochastic gradient descent swinging around the average when the learning rate is high. The economy going through boom and bust around its growth trend. A car bouncing after it goes over a bump. In the Meadows book, a room temperature swinging above and below the setting when the thermostat is far from the heater, and a car dealership's inventory swinging up and down because orders arrive after a delay. Any five of these work.

items.question: A system is described by x dot equals v and v dot equals minus k over m times x. If it starts with x negative and v equal to 0, will it oscillate? Say in a couple of sentences what will happen.
items.answer: Yes, it oscillates. The position x starts negative, so the spring is squeezed and pushes the mass toward equilibrium (x equal to 0). The mass speeds up and reaches 0, but a moving mass keeps moving, so it goes past 0 and stretches the spring on the positive side. The spring then pulls it back, it overshoots again, and this repeats. So the position swings back and forth, tracing out a cosine-shaped wave.

items.question: If x dot equals minus 0.1 times x describes a system, and x starts negative, what will happen? What happens if the number minus 0.1 becomes minus 0.9?
items.answer: The position x rises toward 0 and stops there. This is because x is negative, so minus 0.1 times x is positive, so x goes up. As x gets closer to 0 the change gets smaller, so it rises fast at first and then more and more slowly, and it never crosses 0. With minus 0.9 the same thing happens much faster, because each step changes x by 90 percent of the gap instead of 10 percent. There is no mass in this system, so there is no overshoot and no oscillation.

items.question: In SGD for averaging a list, the formula for the new estimate of the average x is: new x equals current x minus the learning rate times (current x minus the data point d). What is the purpose of the first minus in the formula? Consider the case where the data point is above the current x and the case where it is below.
items.answer: The first minus makes the estimate move toward the data point whether the data point is above or below the current estimate. If the current estimate is above the data point, the difference in the parentheses is positive, so subtracting it makes the estimate go down, toward the data point. If the current estimate is below the data point, the difference is negative, so subtracting a negative number makes the estimate go up, again toward the data point. For example, with an estimate of 130 and a data point of 98, the difference is 32, so the estimate goes down. With an estimate of 94 and a data point of 98, the difference is minus 4, so the estimate goes up.

items.question: What is the math of forward propagation, from the signal input to a neural network all the way to a decision at the end? Describe it.
items.answer: The input signal is a vector, which is a list of numbers, such as pressure values from a sound wave. Each neuron in the first layer multiplies each input number by its own weight and adds the products up. That sum is the inner product, and it is the neuron's activation. The activations of that layer become the inputs to the next layer, where every neuron does the same multiply-and-add with its own weights. This repeats layer by layer until the last layer. The last layer turns its numbers into a probability distribution over the categories, so the numbers are between 0 and 1 and add up to 1. The decision is the category with the largest probability.

items.question: The decision by a neural network is [.1, .1, .1, .2, .5], but the true category is the one in the second position. Using Python list notation, how do we express to the network, as a probability distribution, what the true answer is?
items.answer: The true answer is written as [0, 1, 0, 0, 0]. This is because the correct category gets all of the probability, which is 1, and every other category gets 0. The 1 goes in the second position because that is where the true category is. The list still adds up to 1, so it is a probability distribution, and the network can compare its own output with it to find its mistake.

sets.title: Exam 1 · the 25 questions and the key
sets.about: Given on October 1, 2026. Every question was worth the same number of points, and the space after each question showed how many sentences to write.

items.question: Which of these four could be the probability distribution decision of a neural network? (a) [0, 0, 0, 0], (b) [0, .4, 0, .6], (c) [-.5, 0, .5, 0], (d) [.3, .3, .4, .5].
items.answer: Only (b) is possible. This is because the numbers in a probability distribution have to be between 0 and 1 and have to add up to 1. List (a) adds up to 0. List (c) has a negative number. List (d) adds up to 1.5. List (b) has numbers between 0 and 1 that add up to 1.

items.question: Name three ways in which we can distinguish consonants from each other.
items.answer: Any three of these four. Voicing, which is whether the vocal folds vibrate. Place of articulation, which is where in the mouth the sound is made, such as labial, dental, alveolar, postalveolar or velar. Manner of articulation, which is how the air is constricted, such as fricative, oral stop or nasal stop. Nasality, which is whether the velum is lowered so that the air escapes through the nose.

items.question: One side of the basilar membrane is heavy and not stiff, while the other side is light and very stiff. How do these facts enable hearing?
items.answer: Frequency goes up with stiffness and down with mass. So the heavy, non-stiff end of the membrane vibrates at low frequencies, and the light, stiff end vibrates at high frequencies. Each part of the membrane is hooked to neurons. Those neurons tell the brain which frequencies were heard, based on which location is vibrating.

items.question: Describe how dynamic programming works in terms of the size of problems, and problems containing other problems.
items.answer: You break the big problem into smaller subproblems, and keep breaking those down until you reach small problems that are trivial to solve. You solve those smallest problems first. Then you use their answers to solve the larger problems that contain them, and keep going up until you reach the hardest problem, which is the original one.

items.question: Describe why dynamic programming is more efficient than the exhaustive algorithm.
items.answer: The paths in a shortest path problem overlap. The exhaustive algorithm solves every path separately, so it redoes the same additions over and over. Dynamic programming solves only the non-overlapping parts. It finds the best solution from each state only once and reuses it for every path through that state, so it never repeats work.

items.question: Two vocal tract images are shown. In (a) the tongue tip is up at the teeth. In (b) the lower lip is against the upper teeth. Which of these is f as in family, and which is th as in thing?
items.alt: Two vocal tract images labelled (a) and (b)
items.answer: The f is (b), and the th is (a). This is because f is a labial sound, made with the lower lip against the upper teeth, which is what (b) shows. The th is a dental sound, made with the tongue tip up at the teeth, which is what (a) shows.

items.question: Describe how the stochastic gradient descent algorithm works in your own words.
items.answer: We want to estimate a quantity from some existing data, like the average of a list of numbers. We start with a random estimate. Then we pick a random data point and compute the loss, which is the difference between our guess and that data point. We subtract a small fraction of the loss from the guess, and that fraction is the learning rate. That gives a new, slightly better guess. We repeat this with new random data points over and over, and the guess gets closer and closer to the real answer.

items.question: What is the similarity between n in neck and d in deck, and what is the difference between those sounds?
items.answer: Both are voiced alveolar stops, so they share voicing, place and a complete closure. The difference is that n is a nasal stop, so the velum is lowered and the air comes out through the nose. The d is an oral stop, so the air is blocked completely and then released through the mouth.

items.question: What is the similarity and the difference between the vowels in mean and moon?
items.answer: Both are high vowels, so the tongue is high in the mouth for both. The difference is that the vowel in mean is a front vowel, and the vowel in moon is a back vowel. For moon the lips are also rounded.

items.question: Imagine a stochastic gradient descent algorithm with a very low learning rate, and a springy system with no mass and a low stiffness. (a) Describe how the SGD estimate and the spring's position evolve with time. (b) How would the evolution in time differ if the learning rate and the stiffness increased? For SGD, ignore accuracy and oscillation.
items.answer:
Part (a). Both move toward their goal slowly. With a low learning rate, the SGD estimate only takes a small correction toward the average each time, so it takes many steps to get there. With low stiffness, the spring only pulls weakly, so it drifts back to its equilibrium position slowly.

Part (b). Both would get there faster. A higher learning rate makes bigger corrections toward the average, so the estimate arrives in fewer steps. A stiffer spring pulls harder, so it snaps back to equilibrium more quickly.

items.question: Describe the psychological principle of closure, illustrated by the figure of three black circles with wedges cut out, and how it is used in the GPT system as a principle for learning.
items.alt: Three black circles with wedges cut out that make a triangle appear
items.answer: Humans are very good at filling in missing information using what we already know. In the figure no triangle is actually drawn, but we see one anyway because the brain completes the shape. GPT learns the same way, with the cloze task. It takes a sentence, pretends that part of the sentence is missing, and asks the network to complete what is missing. If the guess is wrong, the weights get adjusted. After billions of these completions the system ends up knowing the language.

items.question: In the shortest path problem shown, what is the greedy forward solution? Write out the numbers with plus signs.
items.alt: A five-stage shortest path graph from A to H with costs on every arrow
items.answer: The greedy forward solution is 3 plus 3 plus 4 plus 2, which is 12, along the path A to B to E to F to H. This is because greedy takes the cheapest arrow out of each state as it goes. From A the cheapest arrow is 3 to B. From B it is 3 to E. From E it is 4 to F. From F the only arrow is 2 to H. The greedy total is 12, and it is not the best path. The cheapest complete path is A to C to D to G to H, which costs 5 plus 2 plus 1 plus 3, which is 11.

items.question: In the same shortest path problem, we call the best cost from any state x to state H V x H. Imagine we have already solved for V D H and V E H. How can I calculate V C H?
items.alt: A five-stage shortest path graph from A to H with costs on every arrow
items.answer: V C H is the smaller of two sums, 2 plus V D H and 1 plus V E H. This is because from C you can only go to D, which costs 2, or to E, which costs 1. Each sum adds the cost of that first step to the best cost of finishing from the state you land in. Taking the minimum is the important part, because the best cost from C is the cheaper of the two complete ways of finishing.

items.question: In terms of accuracy and speed in solving shortest path problems, how do the greedy and exhaustive algorithms compare? And what algorithm do we use if we want to balance those two factors?
items.answer: Greedy is fast but inaccurate, because it only looks at the next arrow and can miss a cheaper complete path. Exhaustive is accurate but slow, because it works out every complete path. To balance the two we use dynamic programming.

items.question: What is my favorite popular way of describing how learning in AI works? Fake it till you make it. Describe why I put it this way.
items.answer: The system starts out with completely random weights, so it does not actually know anything. It is just faking it. It makes a guess, receives feedback, and changes its weights a little so that it does better next time. After repeating this a lot of times, it makes it, which means it has the right knowledge.

items.question: In each vowel, does the air vibrate at a single frequency? Yes or no?
items.answer: No. The air in a vowel vibrates at several frequencies at once, because the tongue shape gives different parts of the air in the vocal tract different mass and stiffness, so they vibrate at different frequencies together.

items.question: What is the goal of a spring, if it is extended or squeezed? What is the primary physical property of a mass that is already moving?
items.answer: The goal of a spring is to go back to equilibrium, its resting position. The primary property of a mass that is already moving is that it keeps on moving. Together these two facts are why a mass on a spring oscillates, because the spring keeps pulling the mass back and the mass keeps going past the middle.

items.question: A system is described by x dot equals v and v dot equals minus k over m times x. If x starts as negative and v is 0, will the system oscillate? How will the position of the mass evolve with time?
items.answer: Yes, it oscillates. The position x starts out negative, so the spring is squeezed and pushes the mass toward equilibrium at x equal to 0. The mass speeds up and reaches 0, but a moving mass keeps moving, so it overshoots and stretches the spring on the positive side. The spring then pulls it back, it overshoots again, and this repeats. The position swings back and forth, tracing out a cosine-shaped wave.

items.question: Two vocal tract images are shown. In (a) the back of the tongue is raised. In (b) the lips are closed and the velum is lowered. Which of these is k as in Ken, and which is m as in men?
items.alt: Two vocal tract images labelled (a) and (b)
items.answer: The k is (a), and the m is (b). This is because k is a velar sound, made with the back of the tongue raised up to the velum, which is what (a) shows. The m is a labial nasal, made with the lips closed and the velum lowered so that air goes through the nose, which is what (b) shows.

items.question: In SGD for averaging a list, the formula for the new estimate of the average x is: new x equals current x minus the learning rate times (current x minus the data point d). What is the purpose of the first minus in the formula?
items.answer: The minus makes the estimate move toward the data point, whether the data point is above or below the estimate. If the estimate is above the data point, the loss is positive, so subtracting it pushes the estimate down. If the estimate is below the data point, the loss is negative, so subtracting it pushes the estimate up.

items.question: Imagine a neural network with many neurons in many layers. One neuron, call it y, in layer 4 is connected to 5 neurons from the previous layer. Every neuron is connected to all the neurons in the previous layer. How many weights does y have?
items.answer: Neuron y has 5 weights. This is because there is one weight on each connection coming into a neuron, and y has 5 connections coming in, one from each of the 5 neurons in the previous layer.

items.question: Continuing from the previous question, y's weights are w1, w2, w3, w4 and w5, and the activations of the 5 neurons feeding it are x1, x2, x3, x4 and x5. How do we write the activation of neuron y?
items.answer: The activation of y is w1 times x1, plus w2 times x2, plus w3 times x3, plus w4 times x4, plus w5 times x5. This is because each incoming activation is multiplied by its own weight, and then all five products are added up. That sum is the inner product.

items.question: The decision made by a neural network is [.4, .1, .1, .3, .1], but the true category is the one in the last position. Using Python list notation, how do we express to the network, in a probability distribution format, what the true answer is?
items.answer: The true answer is [0, 0, 0, 0, 1]. This is because the true category gets all of the probability, which is 1, and the other four categories get 0. The 1 goes in the last position because that is where the true category is.

items.question: If I raise the stiffness of a mass-spring system, does the frequency of vibration rise or fall? And if I raise the mass, does the frequency of vibration rise or fall?
items.answer: Raising the stiffness makes the frequency rise, because a stiffer spring pulls the mass back faster, so each cycle takes less time. Raising the mass makes the frequency fall, because a heavier mass is harder to move and turn around, so each cycle takes more time.

items.question: There are systems all around us. True or false?
items.answer: True. A system is a set of elements with relationships between them that together serve a goal, and that describes speech, an octopus, a thermostat, a population, an economy and a neural network.
